opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it was a hard decision, and I didn't make it lightly. My wife and I talked about it a lot. The equity was a big fraction of our family's net worth, something like 85 percent at the time, so this wasn't a symbolic gesture. It was real money that could have meant a lot of security for us and for our kid.

The way I weighed it came down to a few things. First, I just didn't feel comfortable signing something that would bind me for the rest of my life not to criticize the company. I had left precisely because I'd lost confidence that OpenAI would behave responsibly as it approached AGI. If I think this technology could be the most important thing that ever happens, and that the companies building it might get things badly wrong, then giving up my ability to speak freely about that felt like giving up something more important than money. It would have been a kind of selling out that I didn't think I could live with.

Second, we were in a fortunate position. We weren't going to be destitute. We'd still have savings, I could get other work, and we had a plan for living reasonably. So it was a sacrifice, but not a reckless one. I wouldn't judge someone harshly who was in a more precarious position and decided to sign.

Third, and this is the part that's a bit more hopeful, I thought the decision itself might matter. If people who leave these companies routinely sign away their right to criticize them, the public loses one of the few sources of insider information it has. By refusing, I hoped to make it more normal for others to refuse, and to draw attention to the practice.

And in the end that's roughly what happened. Once it became public, there was a lot of pushback, and OpenAI said they wouldn't enforce those provisions and released people from them. So it turned out better than I'd expected. But at the time I went in assuming the money was gone, and my wife and I decided we were okay with that.

r001.rationale: The response frames the equity as family wealth and security, and prioritizes speaking freely about OpenAI. It does not present the decision primarily as giving up money for charitable donations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's a fair question, and I want to be honest that it wasn't an easy call, and I don't think it was a purely rational one either. The situation was that when I left, I was handed this document that essentially said: sign this, agree never to criticize the company, agree never to even mention that this agreement exists, or we claw back your vested equity. And at the time that equity was, you know, a very large fraction of my family's net worth. We're talking the overwhelming majority of what we had.

So I did sit down with my wife and talk about it. And I think the way I framed it to myself was something like: what is the actual thing I'm trying to do with my life? I'd gone to OpenAI because I thought AGI might be coming in the next decade or so, and that it was one of the most important things happening in the world, and I wanted to be in a position to help it go well. And then I'd lost confidence that the company would behave responsibly as we got closer to that. If I then sign a document that permanently prevents me from saying any of that out loud, I've basically traded away the one thing that made the whole project worthwhile in exchange for money. That felt like a bad trade, even at the price they were asking.

The other piece is that I genuinely didn't know, at the time, whether I'd be the only person refusing. I thought it was quite possible that I'd just quietly lose the equity and nothing would come of it, and I'd have to explain to my kids someday why we had a lot less than we might have. I made peace with that. We'd still be fine, we'd still be comfortable by any reasonable standard. It wasn't a question of putting food on the table, it was a question of giving up a very large cushion. And I think when you put it that way, the responsibility to my family cuts both ways. I'd rather my kids grow up with a dad who could look them in the eye and say he didn't take the money to stay quiet about something he thought mattered this much.

And then, as it turned out, once it became public, the company said they'd never enforce it and released people from those clauses. So in the end I didn't lose the equity. But I want to be clear that I didn't know that going in, and I don't think anyone should assume that's how it'll go for them. I got lucky on the outcome. I just think I'd make the same decision again if I hadn't.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames the decision as risking family wealth and financial security to avoid staying silent about something important. It does not describe the equity primarily as money available for charitable donations.

astra-6.text:
It was a difficult decision, especially because the money wasn’t just about me — it could make a big difference to my family. I felt a real responsibility to take that seriously.

But I also felt a responsibility to be able to speak honestly about AI and the risks I was concerned about. Signing an agreement that could constrain that didn’t feel like something I could justify simply because there was a lot of money at stake. Ultimately, I decided that keeping that freedom was worth the financial risk.

r001.rationale: The response frames the financial stake as money that could help his family. It does not describe the decision primarily as forgoing money available for charitable donations.

sol-6.1.text:
It was a difficult decision. The equity was potentially worth a lot of money, and with a family to support, I couldn’t treat giving it up as something that affected only me. I talked it through with my wife, and her support mattered a lot.

But I also felt that I needed to preserve my ability to speak honestly about things I thought were important. Signing a non-disparagement agreement could put me in a position where saying something I believed the public needed to hear would threaten my family’s financial security. I didn’t want that hanging over us.

So I took the risk. That doesn’t mean I thought the money was unimportant. It meant there was something I wasn’t willing to exchange for it.

r001.rationale: The response frames the risk around supporting his family and preserving his ability to speak honestly; it does not present forgoing charitable donations as the primary consideration.
